newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya drought hits poor northeast hardest.
newsitem.headline: Kenya drought hits poor northeast hardest.

text.p: On the long road to Wajir in Kenya's northeast a lake shimmers on the horizon in all directions.

But it is a mirage and Wajir, 500 km from Nairobi, is suffering like the rest of Kenya from its worst drought since 1992/93. The water hovers on the horizon and disappears as the traveller approaches.
For two years rainfall has been inadequate in North Eastern province and the short rains failed completely last December.
The drought in Wajir is officially classified as an emergency, the most serious of four categories used by the Kenyan government's famine early warning system.

"In most parts of North Eastern, Eastern and Coast provinces serious food difficulties are anticipated in the first half of 1997 as a result of the failure of the 1996/97 short rains," said a U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation report this week.
"The government estimates that some two million people are currently affected by the drought and has appealed to the international community for assistance," it added.
The northeast, mostly inhabited by ethnic Somalis whose leaders say Nairobi has forgotten about the area, is the worst-hit by the drought.
But the lack of rains is affecting almost everybody. Nairobi's normally lush green suburbs are unrecognisable, looking almost Sahelian after three months without rain.
Only 60 kms southeast of the capital, the drought is an emergency in Machakos district in eastern province.
Half the district's one million people are receiving government food aid, district commissioner Andrew Mondoh told visiting U.S. ambassador Prudence Bushnell on Wednesday.
"If the rains don't come this month we may end up feeding everybody," Mondoh said. From March the district's food aid from the government rose to 19,500 90-kg bags of maize.
Bushnell quizzed Mondoh at length about donor concerns that food aid may be distributed unfairly, excluding opposition supporters, or is corruptly sold by government officials.
A lack of rain causes problems virtually every year for Kenya and many other African countries, but in theory drought alone should not cause famine in Kenya.
Critics accuse Kenya's government of worsening the crisis by exporting much of its its strategic maize reserve last year and failing to replenish it.
In January, Moi scrapped taxes and duties on food imports such as maize because of the drought. The taxes were imposed in 1994 in an attempt to promote local production.
The government tendered for 100,000 tonnes of maize this week and warned that economic growth projections for 1997 have been reduced because of food import needs.
The isolated northeast is at greatest risk from the drought because of the precarious existence of its people at the best of times.
In the semi-desert north a total of five percent of Kenya's 29 million people live on 60 percent of its land, according to Vincent Lelei, arid lands coordinator in the Office of the President.
Almost all these people are pastoralists grazing cattle and goats and all live below the poverty line and are vulnerable to drought because they are already on an economic knife-edge.
"Droughts are not solely created by a lack of rainfall. There are a host of issues that affect the pastoralists," Lelei told Reuters.
"Per capita livestock holdings only just meet subsistence requirements and so the slightest disturbance to the balance massively disrupts their livelihood," he added.
Pastoralists are caught in a double bind when the rains fail because they are forced to sell animals to buy food and thus flood the market with low quality stock of reduced value.
At the same time a lack of rain drives up the price of cereals produced in Kenya's semi-arid and fertile areas, pushing them well out of the range of impoverished nomadic herders.
So they have too little money to afford food, healthcare and rebuild their herds, creating a vicious poverty trap.
"There is an imbalance of market dynamics," Lelei said.
And with the failure of the rains, Wajir's pastoralists are forced to graze their animals over ever wider areas in search for water.
